pos: n. (a written bond; a signed certificate of debt)
etymology: Greek cheirographon, literally a thing written by hand — in the commercial Greek of the first century, a signed note of indebtedness, an IOU acknowledged by the debtor's own hand. The Authorized Version keeps the concrete legal image rather than softening it to record or charge.
biblical_def: Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross. Paul reaches for a debtor's bond, and the choice of image is the whole argument. A handwriting is not an accusation made by an enemy; it is a document the debtor himself signed. The law of God, holy and just and good, stood against us not because it was unjust but because we had subscribed to it and failed it, and the bond was in force. Two things are said of that bond, and both are decisive. It was against us — legally valid, properly drawn, enforceable. And it was contrary to us — actively opposed, standing in the way of every approach to God. Paul does not say the bond was cancelled by divine leniency, nor that God overlooked it, nor that it was discovered to be invalid. He says it was blotted out, taken out of the way, and nailed to the cross. The debt was not waived; it was transferred and discharged in the body of Christ, who having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances, made peace. This is why there is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus. The bond is not in a drawer somewhere, suspended. It is nailed up, publicly, spent.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the cast or form of writing peculiar to each hand or person; a writing; anything written; that which is written by hand.
webster_full: HANDWRITING, n. The cast or form of writing peculiar to each hand or person.
HANDWRITING, n. Anything written by hand; a writing; that which has been written.
BOND, n. An obligation or deed by which a person binds himself, his heirs, executors and administrators, to pay a certain sum on or before a future day appointed.
ORDINANCE, n. A rule established by authority; a permanent rule of action; a law or statute.
BLOT, v.t. To obliterate writing with ink; to efface; to erase; to cause to be unseen or forgotten.
scriptures: Colossians 2:14
Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross;
Ephesians 2:15
Having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments contained in ordinances; for to make in himself of twain one new man, so making peace;
Galatians 3:13
Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us: for it is written, Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree:
Romans 8:1
There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit.
corruption_summary: Modern preaching regularly reduces the handwriting to a feeling of guilt and the blotting out to a change in how we see ourselves; Scripture makes it a real legal instrument really discharged by a real death.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic retelling of Colossians 2:14 makes the bond subjective — the accusing voice in a believer's head, the shame he carries, the internalized critic — and makes the cross a demonstration that God never really held anything against him. That is a different gospel with the same vocabulary. Paul's bond is objective, and God is the party who holds it. The cross does not tell us the debt was imaginary; it tells us the debt was paid. A man comforted by being told he never owed anything has not been forgiven, and the moment his conscience wakes he will find the comfort empty, because the bond he actually signed is untouched.

The opposite corruption keeps the legal language but relocates the payment into the believer's own obedience, so that the bond is blotted out progressively as the Christian improves. Rome's system of merit and satisfaction does exactly this, and every revivalist scheme that makes assurance ride on performance does it again in Protestant dress. The text will not bear it. The blotting out, the taking out of the way, and the nailing are all in the aorist — done, finished, at a point in past time, by another. The believer contributes the debt. Christ contributes the payment.
roots_summary: Greek cheirographon (G5498), a handwritten bond; exaleipho (G1813), to wipe out or blot out; dogma (G1378), decree or ordinance; proseloo (G4338), to nail to.
roots_lines: Greek cheirographon (G5498) — a bond written by the debtor's own hand; rendered handwriting at Colossians 2:14, its only occurrence.
Greek exaleipho (G1813) — to wipe away, to blot out utterly; used of blotting out sins and of blotting a name out of the book of life.
Greek dogma (G1378) — a decree or ordinance; the ordinances the bond consisted of.
Greek proseloo (G4338) — to fasten with nails; used only here, of the bond nailed to the cross.
Greek hupenantios (G5227) — set over against, opposed; rendered contrary to us.
usage: “the handwriting of ordinances that was against us” — the bond, valid and enforceable.
“took it out of the way” — removed from the middle, where it had blocked the way to God.
“nailing it to his cross” — the discharged bond posted publicly, as a receipt.

pos: adj. (rational; belonging to the mind; fitting to reason)
etymology: Greek logikos, of or belonging to logos — reason, word. The Authorized Version renders it reasonable at Romans 12:1 and of the word at 1 Peter 2:2. The English word has drifted toward moderate; the Greek means rational, belonging to a mind, as against merely bodily or ceremonial.
biblical_def: I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. The word does not mean moderate, and Paul is not asking for a measured, sensible, proportionate religion. Logikos means rational — the worship of a creature who has a mind and knows why he is doing it. Under the old covenant a man brought a beast that had no idea what was happening to it. Paul says the Christian brings himself, knowingly, understanding the mercies by which he is asked. That is the force of therefore: eleven chapters of doctrine stand behind the appeal, and the appeal is addressed to men who have followed the argument. Two things follow. First, this worship is embodied — your bodies, not your sentiments; the sacrifice is living and walks about. Second, it is intelligent, and therefore inseparable from the renewing of the mind that Paul immediately commands. Be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind. A worship that bypasses the understanding is not the reasonable service of Romans 12, whatever its intensity.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): having the faculty of reason; governed by reason; conformable to reason; just; rational.
webster_full: REASONABLE, a. Having the faculty of reason; endued with reason; as a reasonable being.
REASONABLE, a. Governed by reason; being under the influence of reason; thinking, speaking or acting rationally or according to the dictates of reason.
REASONABLE, a. Conformable or agreeable to reason; just; rational.
SERVICE, n. The act of serving; that which is done in obedience to a superior; also, public worship or religious duties performed.
SACRIFICE, n. An offering made to God; anything consecrated and offered to God or to a divinity.
scriptures: Romans 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
Romans 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
1 Corinthians 6:20
For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.
Psalm 51:17
The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.
corruption_summary: The English drift from rational to moderate has been read back into Romans 12:1, producing a religion of reasonable proportions; and the opposite error strips worship of the understanding altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: Because reasonable now means moderate in ordinary English, Romans 12:1 is quoted for a temperate, balanced discipleship that does not go to extremes. The text says the opposite. The sacrifice is the whole body, presented once and for all, and there is nothing moderate about a burnt offering. What is reasonable about it is that the man understands what he is doing and why — by the mercies of God. Read rightly, the verse forbids exactly the half-measure it is usually quoted to defend.

The contrary corruption is older and more common in the churches: worship that aims at the affections by going around the understanding. The regulative principle stands against it, and so does this word. Where the mind is bypassed — by spectacle, by volume, by manufactured atmosphere, by a liturgy in a tongue the people do not know — the offering may be sincere but it is not logikos. Paul ties the living sacrifice to the renewed mind in the very next sentence, and the two cannot be separated without loss.
roots_summary: Greek logikos (G3050), rational, belonging to the word or reason; paristemi (G3936), to present or offer; thusia (G2378), sacrifice; metamorphoo (G3339), to be transformed.
roots_lines: Greek logikos (G3050) — rational, pertaining to reason; rendered reasonable here and of the word at 1 Peter 2:2, its only two occurrences.
Greek paristemi (G3936) — to place beside, to present; the technical word for presenting an offering at the altar.
Greek thusia (G2378) — a sacrifice, the thing offered; here qualified as living, against every slain beast before it.
Greek metamorphoo (G3339) — to be transformed, changed in form; the same word used of the transfiguration.
Greek anakainosis (G342) — renewing, a making new; of the mind, not the feelings.
usage: “which is your reasonable service” — worship offered by a creature who understands.
“present your bodies a living sacrifice” — embodied, not merely inward.
“by the mercies of God” — the ground of the appeal, and what makes it reasonable.

pos: n. pl. (impulses; stirrings; passions at work)
etymology: Greek pathemata, sufferings, passions, things undergone. The Authorized Version renders it motions at Romans 7:5, catching the sense of an inward stirring set going — not a settled choice but a movement in the members.
biblical_def: For when we were in the flesh, the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death. Paul is describing what the law does to an unregenerate man, and the description is anatomical. Sin is not merely a verdict on the record; it is a set of motions, live impulses, working in the members — hand, eye, tongue, appetite. And the law occasions them. Which were by the law does not mean the law is sinful; Paul denies that in the strongest terms. It means the commandment, coming to a heart in rebellion, stirs the very thing it forbids, so that the prohibition itself becomes the occasion of desire. This is the honest anatomy of total depravity: the fault is not in the standard but in the nature that meets it. Note the tense and the pronoun — when we were in the flesh. The believer is no longer in the flesh in the sense Paul means, though the flesh remains in him, which is why he can still say that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwelleth no good thing. The motions are not extinguished at conversion; they are dethroned, and the Christian is commanded to mortify them by the Spirit.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act or process of changing place; internal action; an impulse communicated; a proposal made.
webster_full: MOTION, n. The act or process of changing place; change of local position; the passing of a body from one place to another.
MOTION, n. Internal action; excitement of the mind, or an impulse or influence operating upon it.
MOTION, n. Tendency of the mind; impulse; as the motions of the spirit.
MEMBER, n. A limb of animal bodies; as a leg, an arm, a finger.
MORTIFY, v.t. To subdue or bring into subjection, as the appetites and passions, by abstinence or severe penance.
scriptures: Romans 7:5
For when we were in the flesh, the motions of sins, which were by the law, did work in our members to bring forth fruit unto death.
Romans 7:18
For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
Galatians 5:24
And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
Romans 8:13
For if ye live after the flesh, ye shall die: but if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live.
corruption_summary: Modern moral vocabulary renames the motions of sin as urges, drives, or orientations — morally neutral facts about a person — where Scripture calls them sin at work in the members, to be mortified and not managed.
corruption_paragraphs: The dominant therapeutic account treats inward impulse as raw data about the self: a drive to be understood, integrated, and expressed, never resisted at the root. On that account the man who feels a motion strongly enough is being told who he is. Romans 7:5 gives the opposite verdict. The motions of sins are sin working, and they are working toward fruit, and the fruit is death. To identify with them is not self-knowledge but suicide. The imago Dei in every person stands; the impulse warring against God does not define him, and the counsel to make peace with it is counsel toward the grave.

The error nearer to the churches is quietism: since the motions remain after conversion, the believer is told to leave them alone and wait for God to do something. Paul commands the exact opposite in the same letter — if ye through the Spirit do mortify the deeds of the body, ye shall live. Mortification is active, daily, and the Christian's own work, done in the Spirit's strength. They that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. That is a settled fact to be made good every day, not a mood to be waited for.
roots_summary: Greek pathema (G3804), a passion or suffering; sarx (G4561), flesh; melos (G3196), a member or limb; energeo (G1754), to work effectually.
roots_lines: Greek pathema (G3804) — that which is undergone; a passion, an affection; rendered motions at Romans 7:5.
Greek sarx (G4561) — flesh; in Paul, fallen human nature considered as the seat of sin.
Greek melos (G3196) — a limb or member of the body; where the motions do their work.
Greek energeo (G1754) — to be at work, to operate effectually; rendered did work.
Greek thanatoo (G2289) — to put to death; rendered mortify at Romans 8:13.
usage: “the motions of sins” — sin considered as live impulse, not bare guilt.
“did work in our members” — the body as the theatre of the conflict.
“to bring forth fruit unto death” — every motion has an issue.

pos: n. (love of wisdom; a system of human speculation)
etymology: Greek philosophia, love of wisdom, from philos, loving, and sophia, wisdom. The word occurs once in the New Testament, and it occurs as a warning.
biblical_def: Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ. Paul is not condemning the use of the mind; he has just commanded a reasonable service, and he argues here with close reasoning. He is condemning a particular thing, and he defines it in the same breath by three marks. It is vain deceit — empty, and it misleads. It is after the tradition of men — its authority is human handing-down, not divine revelation. It is after the rudiments of the world — it works from the elementary principles of the created order as if that order explained itself. And the fourth mark is the decisive one, stated negatively: not after Christ. The danger is not thinking but thinking from a starting point other than Christ, in whom dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily and in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. The verb is worth weighing. Spoil is to carry off as plunder. Paul is not warning of an intellectual embarrassment but of a theft — a man walked off with, made prey, by a system.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): literally, the love of wisdom; the knowledge of the causes of all phenomena; the science which treats of the principles of things.
webster_full: PHILOSOPHY, n. Literally, the love of wisdom. But in modern acceptation, philosophy is a general term denoting an explanation of the reasons of things.
PHILOSOPHY, n. The knowledge of the causes of all phenomena, both of mind and of matter.
PHILOSOPHY, n. Hypothesis or system on which natural effects are explained.
RUDIMENT, n. The original or first principle of any art or science; the first elements of a thing.
TRADITION, n. The delivery of opinions, doctrines, practices, rites and customs from father to son, or from ancestors to posterity; oral transmission.
scriptures: Colossians 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
Colossians 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
1 Corinthians 1:20
Where is the wise? where is the scribe? where is the disputer of this world? hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world?
1 Corinthians 3:19
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
corruption_summary: The verse is pressed into service both by anti-intellectualism, which reads it as a ban on rigorous thought, and by an accommodating theology that treats the reigning philosophy of the age as a neutral container for Christian content.
corruption_paragraphs: The anti-intellectual reading takes Colossians 2:8 as a prohibition on study, logic, and learning, and produces a church unable to answer a first objection. That is not what Paul wrote. He names four marks, and the last is the load-bearing one — not after Christ. A philosophy is condemned by its starting point and its master, not by its rigour. The Reformed tradition has never been afraid of the mind; it produced Owen, Turretin, and Edwards, and it insists that every thought be brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ — which requires thinking, and hard thinking, not less of it.

The opposite and now more common corruption is accommodation. Each generation finds a regnant framework — German idealism, existentialism, process thought, critical theory — and offers it as the neutral language into which the gospel may be translated for a modern hearer. The translation always costs. Process theology surrendered God's immutability and omnipotence; open theism surrendered his exhaustive foreknowledge; critical frameworks replace the biblical anthropology of one-in-Adam and one-in-Christ with an oppressor-oppressed binary. In each case a tradition of men supplied the first principles and Christ was fitted in afterward, which is precisely the thing Paul says will carry a church off as plunder.
roots_summary: Greek philosophia (G5385), love of wisdom; sulagogeo (G4812), to carry off as spoil; stoicheion (G4747), rudiment or elementary principle; paradosis (G3862), tradition.
roots_lines: Greek philosophia (G5385) — love of wisdom; its only occurrence in the New Testament is this warning.
Greek sulagogeo (G4812) — to carry off as booty, to kidnap; rendered spoil, and used nowhere else.
Greek stoicheion (G4747) — an element, a first principle in a series; rendered rudiments.
Greek paradosis (G3862) — a handing down, a tradition; the same word used of the traditions that made void the commandment of God.
Greek apate (G539) — deceit, delusion; joined here to kenos, empty, as vain deceit.
usage: “spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit” — the church as plunder carried off.
“after the rudiments of the world” — first principles drawn from the creature.
“and not after Christ” — the mark that decides the case.

pos: n. (that which feeds and sustains; supply ministered to a body)
etymology: Greek epichoregeo, to supply or minister, underlies the phrase; the noun in the Authorized Version renders the idea of nutriment conveyed through joints and bands. The English comes through Old French norrir, from Latin nutrire, to feed.
biblical_def: And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God. The picture is a body fed from its head, and every term in it is load-bearing. Nourishment is not generated by the members; it is ministered to them, supplied from outside and above, and it reaches them through joints and bands — that is, through the ordinary connective structure of the body, not by private channels. Growth follows: the body increaseth with the increase of God, a growth that is God's own giving and not the members' achievement. Paul states it negatively because he is describing men who had let go: not holding the Head. A member may keep the appearance of life for a while after the supply is cut, but it will not grow, and it will not live. The Lord says the same thing in his own figure — I am the vine, ye are the branches; for without me ye can do nothing. Two practical conclusions follow for the Christian and for the congregation. Nourishment comes from Christ, so no substitute will feed. And it comes through the joints and bands, so the member that detaches itself from the body has cut the very channel by which Christ feeds him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): that which serves to promote the growth of animals or plants, or to repair the waste of animal bodies; nutriment; food; sustenance.
webster_full: NOURISHMENT, n. That which serves to promote the growth of animals or plants, or to repair the waste of animal bodies; food; sustenance; nutriment.
NOURISHMENT, n. Nutrition; support of animal or vegetable life and growth.
NOURISH, v.t. To feed and cause to grow; to supply a living being with matter which increases its bulk or supplies the waste occasioned by any of the animal functions.
MINISTER, v.t. To give; to afford; to supply.
KNIT, v.t. To unite closely; to connect; to join.
scriptures: Colossians 2:19
And not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God.
Ephesians 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
1 Peter 2:2
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
corruption_summary: Spiritual nourishment is widely relocated from Christ ministered through word, ordinances, and the body, to whatever a believer finds personally sustaining; and the joints and bands are treated as optional.
corruption_paragraphs: The individualized account of Christian growth treats the church as a resource a believer may use if he finds it helpful. Colossians 2:19 makes the body the channel, not the accessory. Nourishment is ministered by joints and bands — through the preached word, the ordinances, the oversight of elders, the mutual service of members. A man who has severed those connections has not chosen a leaner diet; he has cut the supply line. The regulative principle is not fussiness about forms but the recognition that God has appointed the means by which he feeds his people, and that no substitute of our devising carries the nutriment.

A second substitution is subtler and comes from within the churches: nourishment identified with experience — the felt encounter, the moving service, the sense of having been fed — rather than with Christ held by faith through his appointed means. Peter says the milk is of the word, and Paul locates the supply in the Head. Where a congregation begins to measure its feeding by intensity rather than by Christ delivered in the Scriptures, it will keep the sensation for a season and lose the growth, because the increase in view is the increase of God and God has said where he gives it.
roots_summary: Greek epichoregeo (G2023), to supply abundantly; haphe (G860), a joint or band of union; sumbibazo (G4822), to knit together; auxano (G837), to grow or increase.
roots_lines: Greek epichoregeo (G2023) — to supply, to minister to; the supply comes from the Head, not from the member.
Greek haphe (G860) — a fastening, a joint; the ordinary connective structure through which supply passes.
Greek sumbibazo (G4822) — to knit or join together; rendered knit together.
Greek auxano (G837) — to grow, to increase; the growth is God's own increase.
Greek kephale (G2776) — head; Christ as the Head of the body, the church.
usage: “having nourishment ministered” — supplied, not self-generated.
“by joints and bands” — through the ordinary connective life of the body.
“increaseth with the increase of God” — growth that God gives.

pos: adv. (from the soul; with the whole inward man)
etymology: Greek ek psuches, literally out of the soul. The Authorized Version's heartily renders a phrase, not a single word, and keeps the Hebraic sense of the inward man as the source of an action rather than merely its accompaniment.
biblical_def: And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. The verse is addressed to servants, and its setting matters: Paul is speaking to men whose labour was owned by somebody else, much of it dull and none of it chosen. To them he says that the quality of the work is to be governed by its true audience. Heartily is out of the soul — the work proceeding from the inward man, not merely passing through the hands. The contrast Paul draws in the parallel passage is exact: not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart. Eyeservice is work calibrated to observation, which slackens the moment the master turns away. Work done as to the Lord cannot slacken, because the Lord never turns away. Two consequences follow, and both cut against instinct. The commonest labour is elevated: whatsoever ye do takes in the field, the kitchen, and the ledger, and Paul immediately adds the reason — for ye serve the Lord Christ. And the Christian's reward is relocated: ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance, from a Master who sees the work no man ever saw. This is the doctrine of vocation in a single adverb.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): from the heart; with all the heart; with sincerity; with zeal; actively; vigorously.
webster_full: HEARTILY, adv. From the heart; with all the heart; with sincerity; really.
HEARTILY, adv. With zeal; actively; vigorously; earnestly.
HEART, n. The inner part of anything; the seat of the affections and passions; the will; the whole inward man.
EYESERVICE, n. Service performed only under inspection, or the eye of an employer.
MENPLEASER, n. One who is solicitous to please men, rather than to please God.
scriptures: Colossians 3:23
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
Colossians 3:24
Knowing that of the Lord ye shall receive the reward of the inheritance: for ye serve the Lord Christ.
Ephesians 6:6
Not with eyeservice, as menpleasers; but as the servants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart;
1 Corinthians 10:31
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
corruption_summary: The verse is pressed into service for career ambition, as if hearty work meant advancement; and the doctrine of vocation is narrowed until only church work counts as service to Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 3:23 is a favourite of the success literature, where it becomes a warrant for excellence as a route to promotion. Paul's addressees could not be promoted. They were bondservants, and the reward he names is the inheritance, given by the Lord, not the master. The verse does not promise that hearty work will be noticed or rewarded in this life; it says the audience has changed, and therefore the standard has. Read as a productivity maxim it loses the very thing that made it bearable to the men who first heard it.

The narrowing error runs the other way and is common in the churches: a tacit ranking in which ministry and missions are service to Christ while ordinary labour is merely permitted. The apostle knows nothing of it. Whatsoever ye do takes in every lawful calling, and the reason given — for ye serve the Lord Christ — is said to slaves at their work, not to officers at theirs. The Reformers recovered this against the medieval elevation of the cloister above the household, and the recovery needs making again in every generation, since the instinct to grade callings is perennial.
roots_summary: Greek psuche (G5590), soul; ergazomai (G2038), to work; ophthalmodouleia (G3787), eyeservice; anthropareskos (G441), menpleaser.
roots_lines: Greek ek psuches (G1537, G5590) — out of the soul; the phrase rendered heartily.
Greek ergazomai (G2038) — to labour, to work at; the verb of ordinary daily toil.
Greek ophthalmodouleia (G3787) — eye-service, work done only while watched.
Greek anthropareskos (G441) — a man-pleaser; one whose audience is human.
Greek kleronomia (G2817) — inheritance; the reward named to men who owned nothing.
usage: “do it heartily, as to the Lord” — the audience that fixes the standard.
“not with eyeservice, as menpleasers” — the contrast, stated plainly.
“for ye serve the Lord Christ” — said to slaves about their daily work.

pos: v. (cut into a hard surface; incised)
etymology: Greek entupoo, to impress or stamp in. The Authorized Version uses the older strong participle engraven rather than engraved, and the word appears once, of the law cut into stone at Sinai.
biblical_def: But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away. Paul is arguing from the lesser to the greater, and the whole force of the argument sits on the word engraven. The law was cut into stone — permanent, external, unyielding, and given with such glory that Moses' face had to be veiled. Paul grants all of it. He calls that ministration glorious, twice. But he calls it the ministration of death, because a perfect standard cut in stone can only condemn a heart that is not made of the same material. The contrast is not between a bad covenant and a good one but between a glory that fades and a glory that remains. Against the tables of stone Paul sets the epistle of Christ, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart — the very thing Jeremiah had promised when the Lord said, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts. The law is not abolished in the new covenant. It changes surface. What was engraven on stone outside the man is inscribed by the Spirit within him.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): cut, as letters or figures, on a hard substance; imprinted; deeply impressed.
webster_full: ENGRAVE, v.t. To cut, as metals, stones or other hard substances, with a chisel or graver; to cut figures, letters or devices on stone or metal.
ENGRAVEN, pp. Cut, as figures or letters, on a hard substance; imprinted.
ENGRAVE, v.t. To imprint; to impress deeply; to infix.
GRAVEN, pp. Cut or engraved; carved; sculptured.
TABLE, n. A flat surface of wood, stone or metal, on which anything is written or engraved; as the tables of the law.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 3:7

But if the ministration of death, written and engraven in stones, was glorious, so that the children of Israel could not stedfastly behold the face of Moses for the glory of his countenance; which glory was to be done away:
2 Corinthians 3:3

Forasmuch as ye are manifestly declared to be the epistle of Christ ministered by us, written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart.
Exodus 32:16
And the tables were the work of God, and the writing was the writing of God, graven upon the tables.
Jeremiah 31:33

But this shall be the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel; After those days, saith the LORD, I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people.
corruption_summary: The passage is regularly made to teach that the moral law is abolished in Christ; Paul teaches that its glory is surpassed and its location moved, from stone outside the man to the heart within him.
corruption_paragraphs: Antinomian readings take the ministration of death and done away as a verdict on the law itself, concluding that the Christian is done with the commandments. The text does not permit it. Paul calls that ministration glorious, and Exodus tells us the writing was the writing of God. What is done away is the fading glory of a covenant administration, not the righteousness the law expresses. Jeremiah settles the matter from the other side: the new covenant is precisely the covenant in which God writes my law in their hearts. A new covenant that abolished the law would have nothing left to write.

The opposite error is to read the engraving as merely external still — to keep the law on stone, so to speak, and set the Christian to copying it by his own strength. That is the religion of the veiled face, and it produces either despair or self-deceit. Paul's contrast is not law against no-law but ink against Spirit, stone against flesh. The Reformed doctrine of the third use of the law holds both: the law remains the rule of the Christian's life, and the Spirit writes it where it can be obeyed, in a heart made new.
roots_summary: Greek entupoo (G1795), to engrave or stamp in; diakonia (G1248), ministration; doxa (G1391), glory; Hebrew charath (H2801), to cut in or engrave.
roots_lines: Greek entupoo (G1795) — to impress or cut in; rendered engraven, its only occurrence.
Greek diakonia (G1248) — service, ministration; used of both covenant administrations in this chapter.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to render inoperative, to do away; of the fading glory, not of the law.
Hebrew charath (H2801) — to cut in, to engrave; used of the writing of God upon the tables.
Greek plax (G4109) — a flat tablet; set against fleshy tables of the heart.
usage: “written and engraven in stones” — the law cut where it could not be altered.
“the writing was the writing of God” — the engraver named at Sinai.
“write it in their hearts” — the promised change of surface.

etymology: Greek aphthartos, not liable to corruption or decay. The Authorized Version uses the form uncorruptible once, at Romans 1:23, and incorruptible elsewhere; Webster (1828) carries the entry under INCORRUPTIBLE.
biblical_def: And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things. Paul is describing the root of idolatry, and he describes it as an exchange. The word uncorruptible is doing the heavy work: it names what God is and what no creature is. He is not liable to decay, not subject to time, not running down — the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever, the King eternal, immortal, invisible. To worship him is to worship the one thing in the universe that cannot perish. Idolatry reverses the transaction with perfect and terrible symmetry: the uncorruptible is traded for the corruptible, and Paul walks the exchange down the ladder rung by rung — man, then birds, then fourfooted beasts, then creeping things. That descent is the argument. Idolatry never holds its level; having let go of the imperishable it slides, because there is no floor under it. The preceding verse gives the verdict on the trade: professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. And the psalmist supplies the plain fact the idolater will not face — their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands. The thing worshipped decays, and the worshipper with it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), under INCORRUPTIBLE: that cannot corrupt or decay; not admitting of corruption; incapable of being bribed or perverted.
webster_full: INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot corrupt or decay; not admitting of corruption.
INCORRUPTIBLE, a. That cannot be bribed; inflexibly just and upright.
CORRUPTIBLE, a. That may be corrupted; that may decay and perish; subject to decay and destruction.
IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.
IMMORTAL, a. Having no principle of alteration or corruption; exempt from liability to death; imperishable.
scriptures: Romans 1:23
And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things.
1 Timothy 1:17
Now unto the King eternal, immortal, invisible, the only wise God, be honour and glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Psalm 115:4
Their idols are silver and gold, the work of men's hands.
Colossians 2:9
For in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily.
corruption_summary: Divine incorruptibility is quietly surrendered wherever God is made to change, suffer alteration, or develop with his creation; and idolatry is redefined as a matter of priorities rather than an exchange of glory.
corruption_paragraphs: Process theology denies divine immutability outright, and open theism, following Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders, denies exhaustive foreknowledge and makes God a learner within time. Both are departures from Romans 1:23, which does not merely say God has not decayed but that he is uncorruptible — incapable of it by nature. The classical attributes are not Greek intrusions into Hebrew religion, as the standard objection runs; they are the plain entailment of the divine name and are asserted here by an apostle in the course of an argument about idolatry. A God who can be altered is a God who can be traded for, and the whole force of Paul's indictment collapses.

The second corruption softens idolatry into disordered priorities — whatever a man cares about most. There is a truth buried in it, but the flattening loses Paul's point. He describes an exchange of glory: a deliberate substitution of the corruptible for the uncorruptible in the place of worship. That is why the ladder descends to creeping things and why the chapter follows with God giving men up. Idolatry is not a ranking problem to be adjusted; it is treason against the only imperishable One, and the remedy is not better priorities but repentance.
roots_summary: Greek aphthartos (G862), incorruptible; phthartos (G5349), corruptible; allasso (G236), to change or exchange; doxa (G1391), glory.
roots_lines: Greek aphthartos (G862) — not liable to corruption or decay; rendered uncorruptible here, incorruptible elsewhere.
Greek phthartos (G5349) — corruptible, perishable; what man is, and what he traded for.
Greek allasso (G236) — to change, to exchange one thing for another; the verb of the idolatrous trade.
Greek homoioma (G3667) — a likeness, a resemblance; the image made like to of the descent.
Greek aphthartos at 1 Timothy 1:17 — the same divine incorruptibility doxologically confessed.
usage: “the glory of the uncorruptible God” — what was given up in the exchange.
“into an image made like to corruptible man” — what was taken in its place.
“birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things” — the descent idolatry never arrests.

pos: adj. (deserving thanks; meeting with favour; gracious)
etymology: Greek charis, grace or favour — here in the idiomatic sense of this is a gracious thing, that which finds favour. The Authorized Version's thankworthy renders the same word it renders acceptable one verse later.
biblical_def: For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully. Peter is writing to household servants under masters he calls froward, and he is careful to define exactly what earns God's favour in such a case. It is not suffering as such. He says so in the next breath: what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? Deserved suffering borne quietly is simply justice accepted. Two things must be present for suffering to be thankworthy. It must be undeserved — suffering wrongfully. And it must be borne for a particular reason — for conscience toward God, that is, out of regard for God himself, not from stoicism, calculation, or lack of options. That second condition is the one usually dropped, and dropping it changes the doctrine entirely. The Lord makes the same distinction: blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake. Peter then grounds the whole appeal where the Christian's comfort actually lies, in the pattern of Christ — for even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps. The servant is not told that his suffering is meaningless, nor that it will end; he is told whose footsteps he is walking in.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): deserving thanks; worthy of gratitude; meriting acknowledgment.
webster_full: THANKWORTHY, a. Deserving thanks; worthy of gratitude; meritorious.
THANK, n. Expression of gratitude; an acknowledgment made to express a sense of favor or kindness received.
CONSCIENCE, n. Internal or self-knowledge; the faculty, power or principle within us which decides on the lawfulness or unlawfulness of our own actions.
WRONGFULLY, adv. Unjustly; in a manner contrary to the moral law or to justice.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring.
scriptures: 1 Peter 2:19
For this is thankworthy, if a man for conscience toward God endure grief, suffering wrongfully.
1 Peter 2:20
For what glory is it, if, when ye be buffeted for your faults, ye shall take it patiently? but if, when ye do well, and suffer for it, ye take it patiently, this is acceptable with God.
1 Peter 2:21
For even hereunto were ye called: because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example, that ye should follow his steps:
Matthew 5:10
Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness' sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.
corruption_summary: Suffering is now commonly treated as meritorious in itself, or else as an evil with no place in a good God's dealings; Peter makes it thankworthy only when undeserved and borne for conscience toward God.
corruption_paragraphs: One error sanctifies suffering indiscriminately, so that any hardship a Christian bears is assumed to be persecution and any consequence of his own folly is worn as a cross. Peter forecloses it in the very next verse: buffeting for one's faults, patiently borne, earns nothing. The qualifier suffering wrongfully is not decorative. A believer who is disciplined for bad work, corrected for a real fault, or disliked for genuine rudeness has no claim on this text, and the sooner he stops claiming it the sooner he can repent.

The opposite and more fashionable error comes from the prosperity teaching and from the therapeutic instinct it feeds on: that affliction in a believer's life signals either deficient faith or divine indifference, and must be escaped rather than endured. Peter's readers were slaves to froward masters with no prospect of escape, and he does not offer them one. He tells them their endurance finds favour with God and that they are following the steps of Christ, who suffered wrongfully in the highest degree. That is not resignation dressed up; it is the specific comfort that the sufferer is not outside God's notice but inside his pattern.
roots_summary: Greek charis (G5485), grace or favour; suneidesis (G4893), conscience; adikos (G95), unjustly; hupogrammos (G5261), a copy or example to be traced.
roots_lines: Greek charis (G5485) — grace, favour; rendered thankworthy here and acceptable at verse 20.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience, co-knowledge; the motive that makes the endurance thankworthy.
Greek adikos (G95) — unjustly, wrongfully; the condition without which nothing here applies.
Greek hupophero (G5297) — to bear up under; rendered endure.
Greek hupogrammos (G5261) — a writing-copy set for a child to trace; rendered example at verse 21.
usage: “this is thankworthy” — what finds favour with God.
“for conscience toward God” — the motive that qualifies the suffering.
“suffering wrongfully” — the condition Peter will not let go.

pos: n. (cunning dexterity; a trick; artful handling)
etymology: Greek kubeia, literally dice-playing, from kubos, a cube or die — and so, by ready extension, the sharper's trick with the dice. The English sleight (from Old Norse slaegth, cunning) is exact, and survives chiefly in sleight of hand. It is not the word slight.
biblical_def: That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive. Paul has just listed the officers Christ gave the church — apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers — and stated their purpose: the perfecting of the saints, the work of the ministry, the edifying of the body of Christ. This verse gives the negative half of that purpose. Doctrinal teaching exists so that believers will stop being children, and the mark of the child here is not ignorance but instability: tossed to and fro, carried about, at the mercy of whichever wind is blowing. The agents of that instability are described with a gambler's word. Kubeia is dice-playing, and the rigged game is precisely the image — a system that looks like chance and is in fact managed. Paul adds two things to it: cunning craftiness, and a deliberate intent, they lie in wait to deceive. This is not honest error. It is a set trap. And the remedy Paul names is neither cynicism nor withdrawal but growth into the Head: speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an artful trick; dexterity in performing tricks; artful practice; dexterous artifice.
webster_full: SLEIGHT, n. An artful trick; sly artifice; a trick or feat so dexterously performed that the manner of performance escapes observation.
SLEIGHT, n. Dexterous practice; dexterity; adroitness.
CRAFTINESS, n. Cunning; artifice; stratagem; dexterity in devising and effecting a purpose.
DECEIVE, v.t. To mislead the mind; to cause to err; to cause to believe what is false, or disbelieve what is true.
DOCTRINE, n. Principles or positions in any science; whatever is taught; that which is held, put forth as true, and supported by a teacher.
scriptures: Ephesians 4:14
That we henceforth be no more children, tossed to and fro, and carried about with every wind of doctrine, by the sleight of men, and cunning craftiness, whereby they lie in wait to deceive;
Ephesians 4:15
But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things, which is the head, even Christ:
2 Corinthians 11:3
But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
2 Timothy 4:3
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
corruption_summary: Doctrinal error is now widely treated as sincere difference to be respected, which leaves the church defenceless against precisely the deliberate trickery Paul names here.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing assumption of the age is that every teacher is sincere and that naming a doctrine false is a failure of charity. Ephesians 4:14 knows better. Paul says of some teachers that they lie in wait to deceive — the phrase describes an ambush, laid on purpose. To treat all error as honest is not charity; it is a refusal to believe the apostle, and it leaves a congregation with no category for the very thing he says will come. The Lord and his apostles warned of wolves in sheep's clothing, false apostles, and men who creep into houses, and no amount of contemporary politeness dissolves those warnings.

There is a second and opposite failure, and mature churches fall into it more often than they admit: the suspicion that never grows up. Paul's remedy for the tossed child is not permanent wariness but maturity — speaking the truth in love, growing up into Christ. A congregation trained only to detect error, and never fed, remains as much a child as the one blown about, having merely exchanged gullibility for a hard edge. The protection Paul prescribes is positive: enough of Christ, taught well enough and long enough, that the trick no longer works.
roots_summary: Greek kubeia (G2940), dice-playing and so trickery; panourgia (G3834), craftiness; methodeia (G3180), a scheme or lying in wait; kludonizomai (G2831), to be tossed by waves.
roots_lines: Greek kubeia (G2940) — dice-playing, the sharper's trick; rendered sleight, its only occurrence.
Greek panourgia (G3834) — readiness to do anything, unscrupulous cleverness; rendered cunning craftiness.
Greek methodeia (G3180) — a laying in wait, a deliberate scheme; also of the wiles of the devil at Ephesians 6:11.
Greek kludonizomai (G2831) — to be tossed by the surge; rendered tossed to and fro.
Greek peripherō (G4064) — to carry round about; rendered carried about.
usage: “by the sleight of men” — the rigged game, not the honest mistake.
“every wind of doctrine” — the condition of the untaught.
“they lie in wait to deceive” — intent, stated by the apostle.
